title: Building a Paragraph --- Plan, Add, Join, Refer Back

lessons.title: en primer lugar — telling the reader the shape before you fill it

segments.text: You can build a sentence that means more than it says. This chapter is about building something longer than a sentence.
mira — the marker that re-tunes what follows.
por ejemplo — the evidence move.
en pri-MER lu-GAR. see reference.
en primer lugar — "in the first place, firstly."
Primer is Latin primarius, "of the first rank" — English primary, prime. Lugar is locus, "place" — English local, locate. Literally: in the first place, and English kept the phrase intact.
Its partners are en segundo lugar and por último, "lastly."
This is not a connective. It does not join two ideas — it tells the listener how many are coming.

That is a different job, and it is what makes extended text followable. A reader who hears en primer lugar knows to expect a second point and holds a slot open for it. Take the phrase away and the same three points arrive as an undifferentiated list.
Signposting is most of what separates a paragraph from a pile of sentences.

segments.instruction: en primer lugar and make a point
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *en primer lugar* and make a point]

segments.instruction: en segundo lugar and make another
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *en segundo lugar* and make another]

segments.text: What Latin words are inside primer and lugar? (Primarius and locus.) What does the phrase tell a listener that a connective does not? (How many points are coming.)

lessons.title: además — adding a point, not adding an item

segments.text: You have también, "also." This is not the same word, and the difference is the same one pero and sin embargo had.
en primer lugar — the signpost before this.
también — the "also" you already own.
a-de-MÁS, and the accent tells you so. see reference.
además — "furthermore, moreover, besides."
Take it apart: a + de + más — "to, of, more." It is built out of three words you already have, and más is the comparison word from the experience chapter.
So it means, quite literally, "in addition to more." Spanish built its heaviest additive connector out of its lightest pieces.
También adds an item: hablo español; también hablo francés. Además adds a point: es difícil. Además, es caro.
The first says one more of the same kind. The second says and here is a further reason, and it is what an argument uses when the reasons are not interchangeable.
That is the same distinction you met with pero and sin embargo: the light word joins inside a breath, the heavy one opens a new sentence and carries argumentative weight.

segments.instruction: which of the two an argument needs, and why
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the two an argument needs, and why]

segments.text: What three words is además built from? (A, de, más.) What does también add, and what does además add? (An item; a point.)

lessons.title: por lo tanto — the word that makes a text hold together

segments.text: Signpost, addition — and now the join that turns a list of points into an argument.
además — adding a further point.
así que — the everyday "so" you already have.
por lo TAN-to. see reference.
por lo tanto — "therefore, consequently."
Tanto is Latin tantus, "so much, so great." The phrase is for so much — given all that, therefore.
You already have así que, which does the same job in conversation. Por lo tanto is its written, weight-bearing form: the one that appears in an argument where the conclusion has to look earned.
Here is the thing this chapter is really about. The English word for what these connectives create is cohesion — the property that makes a text feel like one thing rather than several.

Cohesion is not achieved by the sentences being about the same topic. It is achieved by each sentence carrying an explicit signal of how it relates to the last one: another point (además), a consequence (por lo tanto), a concession (sin embargo), an example (por ejemplo).
Remove those signals and a paragraph does not become wrong. It becomes work.

segments.instruction: a claim, then por lo tanto, then its consequence
segments.source: [YOU SAY: a claim, then *por lo tanto*, then its consequence]

segments.text: What does tanto mean, and which Latin word is it? (So much — tantus.) What is cohesion? (Each sentence signalling how it relates to the last.)

lessons.title: lo cual — pointing back at everything you just said
lessons.gloss: which — pointing back at a whole clause

segments.text: The last piece: a way to refer to a whole idea rather than a thing.
por lo tanto — the cohesion join.
lo que — naming a thing you cannot name.
lo KUAL. see reference.
lo cual — "which", where the which points at an entire preceding clause.
Cual is Latin qualis, "of what kind" — English quality and the -al of equal. The neuter lo in front is what widens its target: not a noun, but everything just said.
Llegó tarde, lo cual me sorprendió. — "He arrived late, which surprised me." What surprised me is not he, and not late. It is the whole fact.

Pointing back at something already said is called anaphora, and it is the other half of cohesion. Connectives say how sentences relate; anaphora lets a sentence pick up what came before without repeating it.

Spanish is precise here in a way English is not. English which can point at a noun or a clause and leaves you to work out which. Spanish splits the job: que and el cual take a noun, lo cual takes the whole idea. The neuter lo is the marker that says "what follows refers to no single thing."
With that, the chapter's four pieces are complete: plan the text, add to it, join it, and refer back within it.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: what *lo cual* points at that *que* cannot]
[YOU SAY: the word for pointing back (*anaphora*)]

segments.text: What Latin word is cual? (Qualis, "of what kind.") What does the neuter lo do to its target? (Widens it from a noun to a whole idea.) What is the name for pointing back? (Anaphora.)
Four pieces, and the point of them is that they only show their value at length. A single sentence never needed any of this.
Build one paragraph out loud, on any opinion you hold. Four sentences, each with its join.

segments.text: Which of the four tells the listener how many points are coming? (En primer lugar.) Which one points back at a whole idea? (Lo cual.) What is the name for a text whose sentences signal how they relate? (Cohesive.)
